query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel, the formation of a dense and adherent magnetite (Fe3O4) passive film mediates the onset or suppression of corrosion. An engineered pre-treatment that promotes formation of this protective film will suppress corrosion degradation in harsh environments at room temperature, while at elevated temperatures the protection diminishes due to increased film porosity or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 (mild, low-carbon) steel with its standard microstructure and surface condition (no pre-existing passivating film).
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface oxidation treatment (e.g., low‐temperature oxidation in an oxygen-rich atmosphere) designed to form a uniform, dense magnetite film versus maintaining an untreated reference surface.
generation.conditions: Expose samples under harsh corrosive environments that mimic high humidity and oxygen-rich conditions, with tests performed at room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (e.g., ~80°C). Chloride and other aggressive species should be minimized to isolate the role of oxygen/moisture-driven corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The quality of the magnetite (Fe3O4) film, characterized by its density, uniformity, porosity, and adhesion to the steel substrate.
generation.mechanism: The well-formed magnetite layer acts as a barrier that limits the ingress of oxygen and moisture, thereby reducing the electrochemical reactions that drive corrosion. At room temperature the film remains stable and protective, whereas at elevated temperatures the film may develop porosity or spall, allowing accelerated corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, samples with the engineered magnetite pre-treatment will show significantly lower corrosion rates and less surface degradation at room temperature. However, at elevated temperatures, the protective effect will deteriorate as the passive film becomes less adherent, resulting in converging corrosion rates between treated and untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel exhibiting standard corrosion behavior under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable when the primary drivers of corrosion are oxygen and moisture (absent aggressive ions like chlorides) and within moderate temperature ranges up to around 100°C; extreme environments or different corrosive agents may involve additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold at which the protective film’s integrity fails and the magnitude of corrosion rate differences under varied conditions remain uncertain and will require empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Q235 steel samples. One set is pre-treated by controlled oxidation in an oxygen-rich atmosphere at a moderate temperature to induce formation of a dense magnetite film. The other set remains untreated. Expose both sets to a simulated harsh environment (e.g., high humidity and controlled oxygen levels) under two test conditions: room temperature (~25°C) and elevated temperature (~80°C). Use standardized exposure durations and replicate sample sets for statistical significance.
measurements: Corrosion rate via weight loss measurements
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization to assess corrosion kinetics
Surface film characterization via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not show significantly reduced corrosion rates and improved film quality relative to the untreated references at room temperature, or if the degradation trend at elevated temperature does not reflect a loss of protective capacity (i.e., the film remains comparably protective), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion [2] .
